DL PR2 - Video Explanation Script (5-10 minutes)

Hi, in this video I am going to walk you through my Deep Learning PR2 project. The goal of this
project is to predict whether a person's income is above or below 50 thousand dollars a year,
using the Adult Income dataset, also called the Census Income dataset. This is a binary
classification problem, so I built an ANN, an artificial neural network, to solve it.

DATASET AND CLEANING
The dataset has around 48 thousand rows, with features like age, workclass, education, occupation,
hours worked per week, and so on. First I cleaned the data. The text columns had extra spaces in
them, so I stripped those. Then I replaced the question mark values with actual missing values and
dropped those rows, since the missing values were only in a few categorical columns like
workclass, occupation, and native country, and I did not want to distort the data by filling them
in with the most common category. I also dropped fnlwgt, since it is just a census sampling
weight and has nothing to do with income, and I dropped the education column since education dot
num already has the same information as a number.

ONE HOT ENCODING AND SCALING
After cleaning, I one hot encoded the categorical columns, so things like workclass and occupation
became separate 0 and 1 columns. Then I scaled the numeric columns like age and hours per week
using StandardScaler, but I did not scale the one hot encoded columns since they are already 0 or
1. I also used stratify when splitting into train and test sets, so both sets keep the same class
balance.

CLASS IMBALANCE
One important thing about this dataset is that it is imbalanced. About 75 percent of people earn
less than or equal to 50 thousand, and only about 25 percent earn more. Because of this, I did not
just look at accuracy, I also tracked precision, recall, and F1 score for the minority class, which
is the people earning more than 50K.

BASELINE MODEL AND SIGMOID
For the baseline model, I built a simple ANN with two hidden layers, 128 neurons and 64 neurons,
using ReLU activation, and a single sigmoid neuron at the output. I used sigmoid instead of softmax
because we only have two classes, so one neuron that outputs a probability between 0 and 1 is
enough. The baseline model got an accuracy of about 84 percent and a class 1 F1 score of about
0.64.

ACTIVATION FUNCTIONS
Next I compared four activation functions for the hidden layers: ReLU, Tanh, Sigmoid, and ELU. In
my run, ELU actually gave the best class 1 F1 score, around 0.67, slightly better than the others.
I also looked at something called dead neurons for the ReLU model, which are neurons that always
output zero. In my run, I actually found zero dead neurons out of 128, which was a nice result. I
also looked at vanishing gradients using the sigmoid model, and I could clearly see that the
gradients got smaller and smaller as you go from the output layer back to the first layer, because
sigmoid's derivative is at most 0.25, so every layer it passes through shrinks the gradient more.

WEIGHT INITIALIZATION
Then I looked at weight initialization. I compared Glorot uniform, Glorot normal, He uniform, He
normal, and zero initialization. Zero initialization performed badly, staying close to the
majority class baseline of about 75 percent accuracy, because when all the weights start at zero,
every neuron learns the exact same thing, which is called the symmetry problem. He initialization
is recommended for ReLU networks because it accounts for the fact that ReLU kills about half of
its inputs. I also looked at the actual weight distributions before and after training for He
Normal and Glorot Uniform, and you can see the weights spread out more after training as the
network learns which features matter.

LOSS FUNCTIONS
For loss functions, I compared Binary Cross Entropy, Mean Squared Error, Weighted BCE, and Focal
Loss. BCE is the standard for binary classification because it penalizes confident wrong
predictions strongly. In my run, Weighted BCE gave the best class 1 F1 score, about 0.68, better
than the plain baseline's 0.64. This makes sense because Weighted BCE gives more importance to the
minority class during training, so the model tries harder not to miss those cases, which increased
recall a lot, from about 0.58 to about 0.83. Focal loss, on the other hand, actually gave a lower
F1 in my run, around 0.54, mainly because its recall dropped a lot.

BATCH NORMALIZATION
Then I added Batch Normalization, which normalizes the output of each dense layer before applying
the activation function, using the batch's mean and variance during training and a moving average
during prediction. In my run, the batch normalized model got the best ROC AUC score of the whole
project, around 0.896. I also tested putting batch norm before versus after the activation
function, and looked at the learned gamma and beta values, which control how much the network
scales and shifts the normalized values.

OPTIMIZERS
For optimizers, I compared SGD, SGD with momentum, RMSprop, Adam, and an explicitly configured
Adam, all using the strongest setup so far, meaning ReLU, He Normal, batch norm, and BCE loss. I
also ran a learning rate sensitivity test, trying different learning rates for SGD and Adam, and
you can really see in the plots how a learning rate that is too small makes training very slow, and
one that is too large can make training unstable.

FINAL MODEL AND RESULTS
For my final combined model, I used ReLU, He Normal initialization, Batch Normalization, and Adam,
trained for 80 epochs. This gave me an accuracy of about 84.4 percent, a class 1 F1 score of about
0.656, and an ROC AUC of about 0.895. Looking at my full results table, if I compare all the
techniques, Weighted BCE gave the single biggest improvement in class 1 F1 score compared to the
baseline, since it directly targets the class imbalance problem, while batch normalization gave
the best overall ROC AUC.

CONCLUSION
So overall, this project shows how different building blocks of a neural network, activation
functions, initialization, loss functions, batch normalization, and optimizers, all affect how well
the model learns, especially on an imbalanced dataset like this one. Thanks for watching.
